summary: A 1970 note with comments on the Host/Host protocol document, by D. C. Walden. It is feedback on a draft of the host-to-host protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 65 records D. C. Walden's comments on a draft host-to-host protocol. He suggests changes to message framing, links, buffer allocation, and how processes detect message loss.

subtitle: D. C. Walden's comments on a 1970 host-to-host protocol draft.

tldr.problem: The draft host-to-host protocol included design choices about message framing, links, buffer allocation, and error control that Walden questioned.
tldr.mechanism: Walden proposes removing marking, simplifying link allocation, adding a sender-selected pseudo-link, matching allocations to receiver buffers, and acknowledging messages end to end.
tldr.outcome: RFC 65 is a set of comments on Host-Host Protocol Document No. 1, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 65 is a set of comments on a host-to-host protocol draft. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: Message Framing and Control
sections.content:
Walden proposes eliminating marking by sending a message leader and its data as two messages, so the receiver does not need to search for where the data begins. He also suggests that control messages use a control socket rather than a special control link.

For long files, he suggests making the maximum message length a common multiple of computer word sizes so consecutive messages can be placed without shifting.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal separates the leader from the message data to simplify processing. It also suggests sending control messages to a socket rather than using a special link.

sections.title: Links and Buffer Allocation
sections.content:
Walden says links mainly identify connections and that a large link count makes finding an unused link difficult. He proposes a fixed total of 32, 64, 256, or another suitable number of links across destinations.

To distinguish connections over a link, he proposes adding a sender-chosen pseudo-link to non-control message leaders. He also argues that buffer allocations should use the receiver's buffer size rather than variable sender-message lengths.
sections.plainLanguage: Walden proposes fewer links and a separate sender-selected value to distinguish messages. He also wants buffer allocations to match the receiving host's buffers.

sections.title: Acknowledgments for Error Control
sections.content:
Walden considers the ERR mechanism complicated and insufficient. He proposes that a receiving process acknowledge every message to the sending process; if an acknowledgment does not arrive in time, the sender can retransmit a saved copy.

He argues this would detect message loss across the process/NCP, NCP/NCP, Host/IMP, and IMP/IMP levels. He says checksums could be added if dropped or changed bits become a problem.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a copy until it receives an acknowledgment. If none arrives in time, it can send the message again.
